sources: Fishes of Australia (Museums Victoria), Family Toxotidae, Archerfishes: shoot powerful jets of water at terrestrial insects, knocking them into the water, hitting prey at more than ten times their body length; the palate groove becomes a tube when the tongue is pressed against it; they also spray bottom sediment to dislodge buried prey; mangrove-lined estuaries and fresh waters from India to Vanuatu and northern Australia; https://fishesofaustralia.net.au/home/family/313

Los Angeles Zoo, Banded Archerfish: adults can fire as many as seven jets of water up to six feet in rapid succession; presses its tongue onto a groove along the roof of its mouth; young archerfish learn to adjust for the refraction of light; lives in mangrove swamps; https://lazoo.org/explore-your-zoo/our-animals/fish/banded-archerfish

Newport C., Wallis G., Reshitnyk Y. and Siebeck U.E. (2016), Discrimination of human faces by archerfish (Toxotes chatareus), Scientific Reports 6: 27523 (Oxford and University of Queensland), reported by Smithsonian Magazine: fish trained to spit at one face picked it out from up to 44 new faces, with up to 81 per cent accuracy; https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/some-fish-can-be-taught-recognize-human-faces-180959340/

beats.say: This fish shoots bugs off leaves with a water gun in its mouth. And it can learn your face.
The archerfish. It lives in mangrove swamps, from India to Australia.
It spots a bug sitting on a leaf, above the water.
Then it fires. A jet of water knocks the bug right into the water.
How? It presses its tongue into a groove in its mouth. A water gun barrel.
The bug never sees it coming.
It can hit prey more than ten times its own body length away.
An adult can fire up to seven shots in a row.
And here's the hard part. Its eyes are underwater. The bug is in the air.
Light bends at the surface. Young fish learn to adjust their aim for that.
It even spits at the mud, to blast buried food loose.
Then scientists showed archerfish pictures of human faces.
They trained them to spit at one face, and they picked it out from up to forty four strangers.
The best scores? About eight times out of ten.
Would you let one spit in your face?
A fish with a water gun, and it remembers your face.
Follow me. Next, a beetle that finds its way home using the Milky Way.
